utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Now we are back to courtroom 1. Yes, I was informed that there was a scheduling issue. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We had scheduled for the 9th of July to hear the testimony of General Miletic, and last Friday, his lawyer advised me that General Miletic, in light of the Chamber's decision to certify the Tolimir appeal concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second -- the first part of today's hearing was not reflected in the transcript. Shall we continue? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll start over, Mr. President. So this is in regard to General Miletic who is scheduled to testify on the 9th of July and you've issued a subpoena to that effect. His lawyer has advised me that General Miletic is requesting that his testimony be postponed until after the Appeals Chamber decides the issue of whether a person whose case is pending on appeal can be compelled to testify during this trial. That's an issue that you've certified for General Tolimir to appeal and we think that's reasonable, and therefore we join in his request that his subpoena be postponed until after that decision is ruled on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning everyone. That's a useful backdrop to the scheduling issue I wanted to raise that arises from that circumstance. I could begin by noting that the rescheduling of General Miletic is hardly unexpected, given the circumstances, but this is not a finger-pointing exercise. Instead, I wanted to alert the Court to the scheduling concern against the backdrop of what I think has been pretty remarkable scheduling throughout the entire process and great efforts by both parties and what I consider to be the relatively inevitable scheduling difficulties that arise as we begin to approach the end of the Defence time and their options for switching witnesses become -- becomes more limited. In this case, to deal with the postponement of Miletic's testimony, the Defence has accelerated or proposed to accelerate the testimony of expert Keserovic, who had already been moved up considerably from the September slot he had been assigned and about which we had been notified previously. So now he is proposed as a witness for next week, giving us essentially a week to prepare an expert witness's testimony. As the Court, I'm sure, is aware, the preparation of expert cross-examination in view of the density of materials involved is a considerable logistical exercise which requires investment of both resources and time. We spoke to Mr. Robinson about that. As the Court is aware, we have, I think to a largely unprecedented degree, been able to reach accommodations where possible. In this case, he indicated that he considers his options for substitution to be limited, but does agree that it would be a fair approach if Keserovic's direct examination were heard and then his cross-examination was postponed for a later and appropriate date. At the same time, I think Mr. Robinson is concerned about incurring the irritation of the Court for doing so, so we're not presenting this as a fait accompli, but indicating to the Court the problem that has arisen. From the Prosecution point of view, we would not be provided with sufficient time to properly prepare through no fault of our own. And so we think this is an appropriate accommodation, provided of course that there is no attempt to do the same thing with the -- any gap that might be left by postponing the cross-examination of Keserovic by moving somebody else up who also generates the same problem. Again, I think we're going to see more and more of this. The -- we were advised this morning of a shift in the witness schedule that may have some impact on the scheduling of witnesses this week. We're doing our best to accommodate those changes and adjust accordingly, even when it involves a tremendous amount of accelerated work by the Prosecution. I spoke with Mr. Costi who has the following three witnesses and he has indicated his willingness to do everything possible and prevent any need for an adjustment of the schedule on his part, but that's quite an extraordinary effort on his part. We'll continue to do so, but we'll alert the Court to situations where that really isn't possible. So that's what I wanted to bring to the attention of the Court. I hope the Keserovic situation can be resolved as proposed. Again, I would emphasise that under these circumstances both parties agree that that would be a reasonable solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic is an expert on what field, if you could remind us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's a military expert concerning the activities in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation as to the submission of Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The problem is that we don't have -- we were lucky to get General Keserovic to come on such short notice to fill the time next week, in fact, he would be arriving this weekend as would any witness who would have to testify during that time slot. And so we don't have anyone to replace him and the Chamber will have to be idle during the period that we had scheduled for General Miletic if we don't hear his testimony, and that's why I was reluctant to agree to anything with the Prosecution because that's the alternative and I leave it to you. As far as we're concerned, we're proposing that he give his evidence and I leave it to you to decide whether the notice that we've been forced to give to the Prosecution, which is much shorter than we would have liked, is still adequate for them to be able to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will consider the issue. Are there any other matters? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one matter. I appreciate that the Court will be considering this issue. I would simply ask that we be advised at the earliest possible opportunity where things stand so we can adapt accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I advised the Chamber by e-mail this morning that the witness that was scheduled for tomorrow, John Zametica, has now declined to testify and will not be travelling to give his testimony. We filed a motion this morning for a subpoena for him, but it will leave us with a shortage of witnesses this week. So I just want to alert you to that and apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, thank you. I don't think you need to apologise where a witness refuses to come; that's completely out of your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we still have Mr. Deronjic, protected witness, Peric, and Mr. Andan for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless there's any other matters, we'll bring in the witness, Mr. Karisik. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours. Morning, everyone. I just wanted to say -- alert you all in advance, I have about 35 minutes left, checking with the Court staff. I wanted to tell you that I will be asking, once I use that time, for approximately another half-hour. I'd already told Mr. Robinson that, just so you know that request is coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karisik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I want to focus on where we left off last week, which is your trip to Zvornik on 16 July 1995 and ask you some questions about that day. Now, in paragraph 38 of your statement you state: "When I arrived in Zvornik, I first went to the CJB, where I was briefed about the situation and problems concerning Zvornik and then I went straight away to the Zvornik Brigade IKM." In the following paragraph you state: "I asked the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Mr. Vinko Pandurevic, to insist during the talks with the Muslim side on the release of the captured police officer" --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think the witness has a problem with his hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karisik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The volume of the interpretation is low, so it's overpowering -- the voice of the Prosecutor is overpowering the volume of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now do you hear me without any problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we try again, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Mr. Karisik. I'll try again. Talking about the 16 July trip to Zvornik is where we left off. In paragraph 38 you stated: "When I arrived in Zvornik, I first went to the CJB, where I was briefed about the situation and problems concerning Zvornik and then I went straight away to the Zvornik Brigade IKM." In paragraph 39 you say that you spoke with Zvornik Brigade commander Vinko Pandurevic at the IKM. And last week you said you might have been there with Vasic. I just want to confirm that for you and help your memory. Dragomir Vasic, in an interview on 10 June 2003, on page 63, 65 ter number 25301 for my friends, stated that he went with you to Baljkovica to see Mr. Pandurevic, so Mr. Vasic also says he was with you that day. And he says to check with Pandurevic whether it is possible to do anything regarding the exchange for the captured police officer. And he said: "Until that moment I think" you, Mr. Karisik, "were in Bijeljina." So you're with Pandurevic at the IKM after being briefed at the police station about the problems in Zvornik. That's what I'm going to ask you some questions about. First of all, let me tell you what Mr. Vasic knew on the 16th when he met with you and you were briefed about the problems in Zvornik. He testified in this trial -- in this court in the Perisic case at T 4685 to 86 that, on the 14th of July in the morning, he met with Colonel Beara in Bratunac. Colonel Beara told him: "Q. What did he tell you, what did Colonel Beara tell you? "A. He repeated that on the next -- that on the order of General Mladic to him was to kill the prisoners and asked if he could set aside some policemen to help carry out this task, the murders, and Mr. Vasic refused." Mr. Vasic continued in his testimony at 6501, that he met Tomo Kovac that same morning, 14 July, in Bratunac. And he stated: "Immediately after the minister's arrival, Mr. Kovac's arrival, I informed him about my meeting and the content of the conversation and the content actually of what I heard from Mr. Beara. "Q. Did he react at all? "A. The minister said that the military prisoners were under the jurisdiction of the army and that was not our job, that we shouldn't interfere with these matters." And then in his testimony Mr. Vasic was asked again, this time by the court, by Judge David, what he told Mr. Kovac. And he said -- the question was: "Did you refer to Minister Kovac all the details of the content of your conversation with Beara in an explicit manner? "A. Yes, I did precisely, the complete conversation in the evening. And in the morning and in the evening I conveyed to Mr. Kovac." And then the Judge asked him what Mr. Kovac said and Mr. Vasic replied: "I can also add that it was his opinion that because of the tense relations between himself and Mr. Mladic and between the army and the police, it was important for us that we were not authorised or that the prisoners were not under our jurisdiction and that it was not really our concern what was going on and not to interfere." And the Judge said: "Thank you very much. No further questions." So on the 14th of July, two days before you go to Zvornik, Vasic knows from the Main Staff security organ that the plan is to kill all the prisoners in Bratunac. He explains that to your superior, the minister, to who tells him: Not our concern, not to get involved. Now, you spoke in the beginning about the jurisdictional differences, but as a professional, is that okay, is it okay for the minister to say that it's not his concern that the army is planning to kill thousands of prisoners held in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about my role, and as a witness I can say that Vasic didn't tell me that at the time. I don't want to comment on the minister's statement. Additionally, the minister never informed me at the time when he told me verbally that I should go to Zvornik in order to try and influence the command and Commander Pandurevic in order to achieve an exchange of a captured PJP member from Doboj. As far as I can remember, Vasic said that it was a huge problem in terms that the column that was leaving was putting the very town in danger --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Stop --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we never discussed any executions or information --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, well, you're jumping ahead to questions I haven't asked yet. I'll ask it again. As a professional police officer, as a career police officer, if the top level of the MUP of the RS learns of a plan to murder thousands of prisoners, is it okay to do nothing? Forgetting about assisting in the transport of the prisoners that day to execution sites. Is it okay to do nothing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really had never been informed by the minister. I was not even physically close to him in order for us to discuss what was wrong or what was right. So in view of me not having that information at the time, it is inappropriate for me to comment upon it today. Any crime that takes place is wrong, that is my personal opinion. As far as the operation carried out by the Army of Republika Srpska - and I said three or four days ago was that I was at the staff at Pale on a completely different mission relating to the Sarajevo theatre of war, you are now telling me that the minister was involved in this affair related to Srebrenica. I don't know anything about that and I cannot comment on the minister's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, when you're at the IKM with Pandurevic, that's on the 16th of July, as you probably know Mr. Pandurevic has been convicted in this Court and here's what the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 1959. They found that assessing all the evidence, the Trial Chamber was ultimately satisfied beyond all reasonable doubt that on 15 July, Pandurevic was told by Obrenovic about the detention, execution, and burial of prisoners in the Zvornik area. So that's the day before you meet with him for hours. Paragraph 1960 of his judgement is similar. "Based on the information conveyed to him ... Pandurevic thus knew that pursuant to Mladic's order, Beara and Popovic had brought a large number of prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik where they were being executed ..."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please speak more slowly in order for me to be able to understand. If Mr. Prosecutor can just slow down. He speaks very fast, thus I'm not able to follow what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll put it very simply and slowly. In Mr. Pandurevic's trial it was found that he knew beyond reasonable doubt by 15 July 1995 that prisoners were being brought to Zvornik, detained, and executed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I could have P00138, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is Mr. Pandurevic's report to the Drina Corps on 15 July 1995, the day before you met with him. And while it's coming up I'll just read out the section. "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain." So all of that backdrop I've given you is the day before you spend hours with Vasic and Pandurevic in Zvornik at the IKM. Are you telling me that when they briefed you on the problems facing Zvornik, they didn't tell you one of the problems in addition to fighting the column was the fact that they were busy executing, burying Muslim prisoners and had been doing so for three days?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be absolutely not, nobody mentioned any executions or burials, et cetera. I am testifying here and I am a witness who cannot confirm that because, honestly, that had not been said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you're trying to get a Doboj policeman back who's been captured. Did it occur to you in that task to say, "Hey, maybe we can exchange some prisoners for him"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mission, so to speak, was to keep insisting that Commander Pandurevic, whom I heard talking via radio with the commander of the opposite side and I don't know the name of that Muslim officer, to have this policeman exchanged for which purpose I was there in particular. I didn't know whether there were any prisoners who can be exchanged for that policeman and who these people were. They may have been such prisoners, but I insisted because I came there as the member of the staff and the head of the police department for -- pursuant to the order of Mr. Minister to put --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You've answered --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- an end to the story --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've answered the question. So you didn't ask them -- you didn't ask Mr. Pandurevic or Mr. Vasic, "Do you have any prisoners here," since Mr. Pandurevic is complaining that the day before -- he's complaining in his report from the day before that thousands have been brought into his area of responsibility? They didn't tell you, "Well, most of the ones around here have been killed, but there were some in Pilica Dom that you drove past on the way down, we could get a few from there still."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, that's a very difficult question to answer. There's been about three questions. Most of it is comment or argument. I would ask that he put a more clear question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Pandurevic tell you that there were prisoners available?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pandurevic mentioned that there were prisoners somewhere on a road as far as I can remember, although I cannot confirm that accurately. But I was not the person who can tell the commander, and the issue of exchange was under his jurisdiction at the moment, how to go ahead with that. It was not my jurisdiction and my authority to tell Pandurevic what to do and what not to do. I was a representative of the Ministry of the Interior. I came to see the commander and I asked him to carry out the exchange of this policeman, and I keep saying that that is all that I knew. I couldn't influence him in terms of how he was going to proceed with this exchange and I heard him talking with his counterpart, the other commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So again -- and we'll move on, but you'll agree with me that your subordinate knew that these mass executions were going on, Mr. Vasic, and Mr. Pandurevic knew that they were going on, and you were briefed on the situation by them but you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. How could he know -- how could he agree with him as to what Mr. Vasic and what Mr. Pandurevic knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because I've just shown him the evidence that they knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But this is not a debate. He's supposed to be testifying as to what he knows, not speculating on what other people have said at one time or another that they knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, would you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your testimony -- I'll just move on. You didn't know anything about the murder operation even on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After spending hours with Vasic and Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Regardless of the time spent with them. I'm explaining as a witness what I was doing in that time with Pandurevic. Vasic came back soon. He was there only to show me the road. I would never have located the IKM without their help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P0522 [sic], please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This will just help us with the time. This is from the 16 July 1995, Pale police forces command staff, approximately 1500. "We were informed by assistant Karisik about negotiations between the commander of the VRS" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you gave the wrong number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P05222, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So, very simply, around 1500 hours that day you inform the Pale staff about these events; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to read it. Can it be enlarged? Yes, this is a dispatch from Pale with a staff member, one Milun, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P05076, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an intercept from half an hour later and it's from the Main Staff, General Miletic most likely, based on the other evidence, calling the Palma, which is Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook at 1530, 1529. And he says: "I have to get permission from the main boss. "Okay. "Well, that's why I'm calling you. "So from the main head of state? "Yes. "That's why I'm calling ... that's exactly why I'm calling." Then they talk about the information they're getting. For time I won't go through this in detail, but the person from the Main Staff says they need Vinko to contact them right away. And our case is that this is about the column going through. So the -- this is not simply about a return of a policeman. There's no mention of that in this intercept. The main head of state needs to give permission before anything else happens. Isn't that what you were also talking about on the 16th of July, whether this corridor should or should not be opened to allow the Muslims to pass through? Because the president's permission is required.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to comment on the dispatches from the Main Staff of the VRS. The dispatches most likely exist, this is one of them. I don't want to comment on it as an eye-witness of those events because I never saw it. As for the corridor being opened, this was not within my jurisdiction, it was not up to me to decide about that. It was within the purview of the Army of Republika Srpska, which was in charge of the entire operation including the opening up of our stretch of the front in order to allow the forces to leave Srebrenica in the direction of Kalesija and Tuzla. Therefore, there is no need for me to comment on it, nor can I really comment who would be reporting to whom within the army and what their respective competences were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. In your statement at paragraph 62, you say you don't remember if you had direct contact with Mr. Karadzic that day. Mr. Karadzic in this trial stated at 26265, lines 1 to 4: "Thank you. Did you perhaps find out that Mr. Karisik phoned me to inform me of this move of Pandurevic's?" Does that help you remember that you called and spoke with Mr. Karadzic directly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, unfortunately not. My technical capacities were very poor. I was in a mountainous area and I wasn't really able to sit down and have a conversation with Mr. Karadzic, truly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you would have to go through Zvornik on the way back and in Zvornik they had communications directly with Pale. You could have gone right to the CJB and used either the public security or the state security communication lines. But if you don't remember, then fine.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have D02002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were shown this by the Defence in making your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you have the date for the transcript page 26265?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 14 March 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You discuss this in paragraphs 61 and 62 of your statement. This is an intercept between somebody at the Main Staff, we'll probably see it's General Miletic when he comes, and General Mladic. And he says -- it's at 1615, so shortly after 45 minutes later than the one we saw previously. And he says: "Well, the president called a short while ago and said that he had been informed by Karisik that Pandurevic had arranged passage for the Muslims over to the territory." And then he talks about how he said he urgently needs a report from Pandurevic. So again, does that refresh your recollection that you spoke with President Karadzic and gave him realtime information on what was happening with the Muslims in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This isn't about the Muslims in Zvornik; rather, this is about the column which is making its way through. And the question twists the meaning. This is about me making sure that Pandurevic was not punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Nicholls was referring to the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was exactly, and I think it's not a fair comment for him to now give his explanation of what this conversation was about to the witness. Whether it is -- it is exactly about the column which was in Zvornik, which was made up of Muslims. So my question was precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it might have been confusing on the -- shall we continue. Do you remember the question, Mr. Karisik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already answered the question. This is of no particular assistance to me. At the IKM I didn't have the communications necessary to pass on information to anyone. I especially don't recall talking to President Karadzic. Perhaps somebody else, but me at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Well, how did you get the information to President Karadzic about the column which Mr. Karadzic in this trial said that he was called by you and in this intercept it says that he was called by you. Forget about how -- whether you spoke to him directly. How did you get the information to him about the situation in Zvornik so that he had it before 1615 on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my testimony I've been saying that I was not the man who was reporting on operation Srebrenica to President Karadzic at any point in time. I especially don't recall about this because there I was only negotiating with Mr. Pandurevic to bring about the exchange of that policeman. I don't recall discussing anything with President Karadzic. I only spoke in the past tense and I was to report on the Sarajevo battle-field, and then I went to Bijeljina and then I was supposed to attend these negotiations on the order from the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, again, it says here from the Main Staff to Mladic on 16 July at 1615: "Good day, General, sir. Well, it's like this. I've just sent a telegram to Toso. Well, the president called a short while ago and said that he had been informed by Karisik that Pandurevic has arranged passage for the Muslims over to that territory." So you did report on Srebrenica events to the president; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are commenting on an intercept in the Main Staff of the VRS. As a witness I'm telling you that I did not report to President Karadzic and I don't recall that at all. I could not, it was not possible for me, because I did not have the technical requirements for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're -- just agreed to me that you reported to Pale by 1500 on the situation of the policeman. Pale is where the president is.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was an assertion you made. I've been telling you the whole time that I did not contact President Karadzic once when it comes to reporting. When I told you about the information involving the staff in Pale and that short visit which I commented upon earlier on, well, I did tell you what I was able to comment or to report to him about because I was in charge of that Sarajevo area. At any rate, this was within the competence and the decision-making power of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So when Karadzic said in this trial on 14 March 2012: "Did you find out that Mr. Karisik phoned me to inform me about this move of Pandurevic's and to ask me to give him protection," et cetera, that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony I'm speaking about the role I played in that part of the story. I said that I could not confirm that I informed Mr. Karadzic about anything. Without wishing to comment on what the president said at trial. That's a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's because of your technical abilities, but again I'm going to press you on this. You agreed with me just a short while ago that you did report to Pale at 1500 on the situation of the prisoner. So you could report to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, evidently there is a dispatch in which I said that the exchange was ongoing. Was it after my return and upon my return to the base, to the HQ of the department, I can't recall. It was a long time ago, but it is possible that I informed someone about the fact that the negotiations were ongoing and that I was unable to bring about the exchange of the policeman through the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's been so many years. It's difficult for me to recall and there had been thousands of dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll move on in a minute, but are you seriously saying that the highest officer in public security under Tomo Kovac goes all the way down to Zvornik on the 16 July 1995 only to talk about the return of one Doboj policeman, that you weren't there because of the problem of this Muslim column escaping. That's why you were there, weren't you, to inform the president what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is three questions in one there. I do not accept any of your assertions. I truly went there only to bring about the exchange of the policeman. I repeat, the opening up of the corridor is not part of my purview at all. It is within the purview of the military commander and the VRS. My role was specifically defined by the minister and that was to go there in order to make sure that the policeman is exchanged, nothing more and nothing less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've used my 35 minutes. I'd request half an hour more, and I can tell you the topics if you wish or just request it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to -- we've talked about what the MUP didn't do a bit in investigating the crimes committed in Srebrenica, and you explained at the beginning about the jurisdictional issue from your perspective. I want to look at what the MUP did do in relation to the crimes committed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P04491, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that the Trial Chamber's seen before. It's dated 16th of January, 1996. You'll want to read this whole thing. And at the top we see MUP Ministry of the Interior Republika Srpska, office of the minister, Pale. And we see public security department - head, the RJB, so that's you, and it's about a Main Staff dispatch. And it says: "Please find enclosed the full text of a dispatch from the Main Staff sector for intelligence and security ..." et cetera. "To the minister of the interior, the minister, personally. "Considering that we have a group of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who are foreign citizens or are on a list of individuals who have been indicted by The Hague Tribunal, we ask that you order the Bijeljina MUP to issue personal IDs with Serbian names and last names to these individuals or with different first and last names for Serbian nationals, there are 8 (eight) such individuals." Tell me when you've read it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you to have time to read this through? It's the first time I'm seeing it, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can it be blown up just a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We just collapse the English for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take your time. Are you still reading?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, there's been testimony in this trial - 27 February 2012, Your Honours, at T 25351 - by a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, who admitted taking part of mass executions in Branjevo Farm and that members of his unit took part. And that man also testified that indeed around this time he went to Bijeljina and was issued with a fake ID. So my question to you is: Doesn't this show that this strict separation between the army and the MUP regarding Srebrenica events breaks down, doesn't it, when the army needs help covering up the crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way, Mr. Prosecutor. This is your usual co-operation between two state agencies, specifically the intelligence administration of the Main Staff headed by, from what I can tell, Colonel Salapura, and the Ministry of the Interior, headed by the then-minister, who as part of customary co-operation, which I'm sure had nothing to do with Srebrenica, had to meet the request of issuing a number of identity cards which are used in all services and is the customary practice across the world --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- obviously this was part of the public security department and a request was sent, and it was my duty to act upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, usual co-operation, I'm not sure how careful you read this even though you had plenty of time. Is it usual co-operation between the MUP and the VRS to issue false IDs to persons who are on a list of individuals who have been indicted by The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In retrospect I can't tell whether the Law on Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal was being applied at the time. This is for a legal expert. But I do know that our duty was to implement a request coming from our minister. I don't know who these individuals are, I was never interested in that. I heard from you now that these were people from the Main Staff and that they had to do with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait, wait --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- my sphere of interest --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait, you didn't hear from me -- you did hear from me -- it says on this document "members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, this means nothing. I don't know who members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment are as a member of public security. The intelligence administration asked the Ministry of the Interior to pursue activities that were part of your standard co-operation, and I had a role to play in meeting the request sent to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So there were eight fake IDs requested for members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. There were eight members, I'll tell you the evidence shows, of the 10th Sabotage Detachment at the Branjevo Farm's executions. And, if I understand you right, you're telling me these IDs were issued by your department?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them were issued. I wasn't following up on how this was seen through. I'm discussing the dispatch now. Upon an order from the minister, I am pursuing certain activities within the department. I don't know how this went through, whether anything was issued or how many IDs were issued. I do know that I was duty-bound to pass this on pursuant to an order from the minister, that was indeed the case. Now, as for the particulars, this is the co-operation between two state agencies, specifically the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior. I'm sure that somebody else would be better placed to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I want to now talk to you about the one and only MUP investigation in 1995 in connection with the Srebrenica executions, and that is the arrest and prosecution of a journalist for reporting on the executions and attempting to get more of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have paragraph 42, please -- excuse me. 65 ter 21889.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We don't have a copy in your language, sir, so I'll just tell you what this is while it's coming up. It's an article from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: E-court page 1, 65 ter 21889.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's an article from a United States newspaper called "The Christian Science Monitor" from August 18th, 1995. So about a month after you were at the IKM in Zvornik. And the headline is: "Evidence indicates Bosnia massacre." And the sub-headline is: "Eye-witness reports supports charges by US of killings." And the first paragraph refers to "strong evidence that a massacre of Bosnian Muslim prisoners took place last month." The article is by David Rohde. Now, you wouldn't have seen or known about this article, right, because you didn't hear about any crimes committed against Bosnian Muslim prisoners until after the war was over; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this? It will -- I'm going to ask some more questions about Mr. Rohde and this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I notice that a lot of different articles in this document, so I think if we limit it to the first page, then that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the admission at the end of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's fine, thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- and I agree, just this particular article that's on pages 1 and 2, it should be. Could I have P05227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You're done with this article?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the time I don't want to go through all the content. It's just to establish that it was known that David Rohde had published an article alleging massacres of Bosnian Muslims on August 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But let us see how -- yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask. I'm not contesting anything; however, I have not been allowed to tender documents of which the witness has no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I'm -- I suggest dealing with this later on. Probably something more is coming with respect to David Rohde. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is an article -- a report from 31st October 1995. So it's approximately two months after the article I just showed you. And it's from Dragan Kijac, head of RDB, to the VRS. And it is talking about the arrest of David Rohde in Zvornik. Take a chance to look at it. On 29th October 1995, it says in paragraph 2, he "headed for locations where, according to his information, there were mass graves of Muslims killed during the period of combat operations in the Srebrenica area in July this year." And they found military maps, et cetera, and is provided for their action. So what the MUP is concerned with and focusing on a few months after the fall of Srebrenica is not investigating the perpetrators of the crimes, investigating what happened; it's investigating a journalist who's trying to find out what happened. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear from this dispatch that this is information which was sent by the state security department. I would not want to proffer any comments. You should ask the witness who's from that department, from the state security department. I've not seen this dispatch before and I'm really reluctant to provide any comments on other people's dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me show you one more and I'll ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 25253, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. This document is signed by Goran Radovic. We saw earlier some of his reports that were going to you early on in the Srebrenica operation, and it's a detention order for David Rohde. So again - I know it's not your department - but you were a very senior lifetime officer in the RS MUP. Why is it that what the MUP is focusing on and its only prosecution, unless you can -- in its only investigation, unless you can show me another one, after the fall of Srebrenica regarding the murder of Muslims is a journalist who is trying to take pictures of execution sites?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I will not comment upon the dispatch because this was sent by the chief of the state security department. I as the chief of the national security would not like to comment upon this. I've not seen this before. And as far as the criminal report is concerned, I'm sure that it was filed in keeping with the Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners or some other law that concerned the journalist and the journalist was doing things contrary to our laws. I'm sure that the state security department filed a criminal report for that reason. I really don't want to comment because I'm not familiar with the details of the places that are mentioned. I'm sure that he did something that was contrary to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was not national but public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You tell me one investigation by the MUP in 1995 into any of the crimes committed after the fall of Srebrenica that you as head of public security know about.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for that period shortly after the war when we still did not have detailed information that you're presenting here. The information that we had at that time was very weak and insufficient. When it comes to war crimes during those operations were to be dealt with the military prosecutor -- prosecution, it was within their authority. When it -- it was difficult for the Ministry of the Interior to do anything more than that during that period of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I understand that when Tomo Kovac and Vasic hear from somebody on the Main Staff that the Main Staff is going to kill all the prisoners, that the procedure in Republika Srpska, the procedure in that state, was that the military is meant to investigate itself. That's what you're saying, right? You just leave it to them and don't worry about it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We as the Ministry of the Interior learned about those alleged crimes that you mentioned very late, and it seems that some of those crimes indeed did happen. That was within the jurisdiction of the army and the military courts. When it comes to crimes that were committed during all sorts of military operation, the Ministry of the Interior did not have capacities to open that issue, especially in view of the belated information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what about the information received immediately about the role of the MUP in transporting prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik, what about the information available immediately that the MUP had executed over a thousand prisoners on 13 July? Why are there no reports by the MUP of the MUP's involvement in the crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP was resubordinated to the Army of Republika Srpska during that operation. The word "resubordination" means something -- means that we were a minor force that participated but the operation was commanded by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. We were the second-rate force, and it is obvious that something happened that was not supposed to happen or was indeed happening at the time. So when I say it was within the jurisdiction of the army and military courts, you must understand, it has to be clear what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, well, what I'll put to you is the reason the MUP didn't do any reports on the crimes committed by the army or by members of the MUP is because the MUP was part of this criminal operation and, just like the army, didn't investigate itself.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the question that you are putting to me as a witness is something that you should ask the minister of the interior when he comes to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender that document? I only have a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I don't think this has managed to elicit any comment from the witness that either confirms or contradicts his evidence and -- or the document. And going back also to the newspaper article, I think it's -- falls into the same category. I thought Mr. Nicholls had more of a link between David Rohde's situation and this witness, but he doesn't. But he'll have other witnesses which he'll have an opportunity to discuss these things with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I have a couple more documents that don't link directly to this witness, but I think it's pretty incredible and I think it's fair to admit them just to show that the highest-ranking official in the public security department claims not to have known that the only investigation into Srebrenica was part of a cover-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can add one point, Your Honours, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He did comment on these documents and said he -- first that he didn't want to comment, but then said words to the effect: I'm sure this was all legal and this was done in the way that the RDB does things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Based upon this latest comment of Mr. Nicholls with which we agree, we think we have a basis to admit these. We'll admit them both. But the first one -- article is limited to the first and second page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 21889 will be Exhibit P6422 and 25253 will be Exhibit P6423.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, sir, just a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 25254, please. This is again from Goran Radovic to the court in Zvornik, a request to initiate criminal proceedings against David Rohde. I'd like you to focus on the bottom paragraph, II, where it discusses his crime, which included: "In the area of the red mud dam in the village of Petkovci, he shot images of the wider area of the dam with his camera although it was forbidden ..." Now, the dam in Petkovci is an execution site, we say. So when the MUP arrests a foreign journalist who's got military maps, who's got pictures of a dam because he's looking for execution sites, regardless of whether his actions in taking the photos were legal under the law then, you said you didn't have any information. Why does the MUP prosecute the journalist instead of following up on his information and trying to find out clues of what happened at the red dam? Why weren't you informed about this? And I'll make the question very simple for Mr. Robinson. Why weren't you informed about this in public security and told: We've got to investigate a possible execution site at the red dam in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same. The dispatch which was sent by the state security department is something that I don't want to comment upon. I was the chief of the public security department, and all the questions that you have for me perhaps would be better for a witness who comes from that department, from the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you worked -- you're in the diary several times, many times, with Dragan Kijac, head of state security. This dispatch doesn't go to you but it's in Zvornik. This man is arrested in Zvornik, he's held in the Zvornik police station. Why doesn't the MUP -- I'm asking you as a professional, not -- specifically this: When the MUP receives information that there's a possible execution site, why didn't the MUP go out there, look for shell casings, look for bone fragments sticking out of the ground, look for Muslim IDs, and the other type of information they could have found there, instead of prosecuting the man who told them about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we get the reference as to where does it say that in this document? He was arrested for travelling with forged documents and illegal taking of photos of facilities that are not supposed to be photographed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's very clear - I don't have time to go through all the documents - that Mr. Rohde and the other ones here says that he was looking for these -- it says in the first document that I showed that he was looking for crimes committed against the Muslims, the one from Dragan Kijac. This one says he's taking pictures of the red dam at Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Mr. Karisik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not provide any further comments because this concerns the state security department. This is about a disciplinary procedure. It seems that a person violated the law. He was a foreign national and he violated the laws and regulations which concern unlawful photography of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a vital object or facility such as a dam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure if I understood your answer. You said, "I would not provide any further comment ..." Is it because it's other organ's purview or you did not know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was within the purview of a different body, which is why I'm reluctant to provide any comments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then -- no, just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and on top of that, I have to say that I have not seen the document before, so my knowledge of it is limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was other organ's purview and you didn't see it before, but you knew about it; is this what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just wondering when you said "knew about it," that was somewhat vague to me. Did you mean to ask him whether he knew about the arrest and prosecution of the journalist or about this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was asking, Mr. Karisik, whether you knew or heard about the arrest and prosecution of this journalist at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honours, for the same reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We admitted the previous two, and on that basis, we'll admit this as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll speed it up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the 8th of November, 1995. Public statement. "On the basis of his constitutional and legal powers, President of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, made a decision today to acquit American journalist David Rohde of prosecution." And it describes part of his offence as "photographing military and other buildings deep in the territory of our republic." So President Karadzic pardoned, abolished, acquitted, whatever you want to call it, David Rohde for his crime of taking pictures of military institutions like the red dam, and you still say you didn't know about it, head of public security?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the chief of the public security centre. I was the chief of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Same question.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I did not know about this public statement. This was within the purview of the president of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Karadzic. It is clear from the document, and I have no comment on this document. He acted within the purview of his authorities and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 25259.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an "Oslobodjenje" article of 15 November 1995. It's a press conference with your boss, Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I believe, if we can blow it up, it's the section on the right, that whole section on the right, that big column. And if we go to page 3 of the English, please. So one of the questions asked by a journalist was about arresting American journalist David Rohde and Minister Kovac responded. And I won't read it all. But Mr. Kovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you're not going to read it all, you need to make sure the witness can read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that we can blow it up, if you could locate the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe it's the section on the -- it's the last column, if I have it right, under that heading there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that right, sir, the part -- can you read the part about David Rohde?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am still looking for the passage. The letters are really very small. Where is it? Now I can see a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, what Mr. Kovac said was, in part: "Your colleague was performing the most difficult form of espionage for which the sentence from 3 to 15 years of prison is foreseen in Republika Srpska in peace time, so consider it yourselves." I'll skip a sentence. "We will not and cannot accept people who are working outside of their journalist etiquette and openly against my people and this state." I'll skip another sentence. "Rohde was lucky that the negotiations were in process so that our President Karadzic released him by abolition to avoid the pressure on our delegation and the Serbs being blamed for everything." Have you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. However, I am still waiting for a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. And I was just waiting to make sure you'd read it. So my question for you is: Tomo Kovac, your boss, at the very top of the MUP of the RS knows all about the David Rohde situation, he knows he's been abolished. He calls what he's done a serious crime. I'm asking you again, why is it -- from your perspective as a career law enforcement officer, why is it that the only investigation by the MUP in 1995 connected to the crimes committed against Muslims after the fall of Srebrenica is to prosecute a journalist?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you have just confirmed what I already said. This was within the purview within the minister. I don't want to comment on any of his interviews in principle. There is just one sentence here which I would like to quote. Obviously the journalist was in breach of the law. I as a professional mentioned that in one of your questions, or rather, in one of the answers to your questions, and that's why he was prosecuted by our judiciary organs. And I have no further comments on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we basically see Kovac warning other journalists not to follow Rohde's example. I'll put it to you, this is just another example of the MUP engaging in the cover-up of the crimes, the top of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. You will have to ask the minister what it was that he stated and why, but I can't agree with you that the MUP ever covered up any of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I take it you have some re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder of today, we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Lattanzi being away due to her official duties. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Karisik.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you that since we speak the same language, we have to make pauses, and feel free to warn me as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have 505222.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: P05222.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell us what were we requested to carry out as a counter-measure in order for this captured policeman to be released? I'm referring to the last paragraph. I believe that's where it is stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This obviously has to do with the goodwill of the opposing side. They had captive one of our police officers and I'm quite sure that along with that, at least according to this dispatch, they had several prisoners. I'm referring to the Muslim forces that were leaving in a column or in some other location. And I'm talking about the return of our captured fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was our part of the bargain, of the deal, what were we supposed to do in order to have our people released?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably opening up the corridor to free a certain distance of the line in order for the forces to leave, and I spent several hours looking at the civilians and soldiers crossing the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is mention in this dispatch that they wanted their prisoners to be exchanged for our prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about that specific portion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the dispatch, General. Do they mention anything else in this telegram apart from our abiding by our part of the deal, that is, to let them pass through?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, their only goal was to get out and move towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned several reports, or rather, pieces of information, and I suppose that apart from information there is other information that you have to act upon. Did you receive any such information that you had to act upon?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't quite understand your question. What do you have in mind specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 93, last week, you said that there was information containing report. What was the essence of this information? Why was it called information and is there any kind of other form of information?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned several information report of the state security department sent to the public security department relating to the movement of a large group of Muslim fighters breaking through towards Tuzla and Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose that you saw a large number of various reports and documents. Was there any mention in any of those reports any executions of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, throughout this whole period there was not a single report, either in the form of a dispatch or any other form of information report, that any executions took place in the period in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 75 and 89 it was suggested to you on page 75 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wonder if Mr. Karadzic has the correct page references, if he's talking about last week now, rather than page 75, if he has them. It's better for the record to put the official transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I told him last week if he has not access to the updated LiveNote, it would be okay to refer to the page number for the day. But, Mr. Robinson, if you could help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Dr. Karadzic doesn't receive the daily transcripts in the way that we do, so he doesn't really have access to the completed transcript. He's working off of the LiveNote page numbers as he's hearing the testimony and making his own notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could think about a way whether that situation could be improved. In the meantime, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But that depends on the Registry, if they provide me with page numbers like all the other parties have; otherwise, I receive daily page numbers, on a day-by-day basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on Thursday that was on page 75. It was relating to our meeting on the 11th of July, I suppose at 1530 hours, and then again on Thursday, on page 89, it was suggested that Srebrenica was an exceptionally important campaign - these are literally the words used by the Prosecutor - and that there must have been some talk between the two of us about such an important campaign. What was the situation on other fronts and to what extent was Srebrenica important? In other words, what was your priority? Which was more dangerous?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a witness, I can say that my priority was the police forces relating and connected to the Sarajevo battle-field. That was the situation in the Serbian part of Sarajevo and the Romanija Corps. At the time, the Muslim forces launched an offensive in order to break through the defence lines controlled by the Serbian side. There was danger every day that these lines would be broken through and that it would result to a real massacre of the Serbian population in the Serbian part of Sarajevo protected by the Serbian defenders. My role in the staff at Pale -- and the staff in Pale was anyway in -- set up due to the fact that the state of an imminent threat of war was declared in the area, I believe that I and the majority of my colleagues didn't know anything else and that Srebrenica just popped up out of nowhere. But I personally was involved in the Sarajevo battle-field due to the fact that the situation was very difficult, and it was particularly difficult at the connecting point between the Herzegovina Corps and the SRK, where the ministry forces of MUP were resubordinated to VRS, most often the PJP companies of the Ministry of the Interior. The terrain there was very difficult and not easily defendable, and very often they managed to break through our defence positions and then we had to retrieve them again and again. So the situation affecting both the army and the civilians was very serious because the offensive launched by the Muslims was very serious because it was directed towards Ilijas and also the western part held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D9121 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, General, what was the strategic significance of preserving the Serbian Sarajevo? Can you make a comparison between it and any other battle-field and what would the fall of Sarajevo entail?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to make any comparisons of the sort because it is a densely populated area, lots of civilians, approximately 150.000 Sarajevo Serbs would be forced to become subject of exodus and massacre because the position for arranging for an evacuation was extremely difficult and the fall of any municipality would have a domino effect on the fall of other municipalities as well and eventually a terrible plight of the Serb civilians of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I don't have the Serbian version. This is the foreign service of SRNA agency. The date is the 7th of July, 1995. The first, the second, the third piece of news is: [In English] "... Lukavica were under fierce Muslim heavy machine-gun fire --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Quoting, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you to start the quotation because you -- in the first part you overlapped with your -- with the translation of your B/C/S words.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] "In two-day Muslim attacks on Serb Sarajevo, five civilians were killed and four wounded, announced the Information Service of the Army of Republika Srpska headquarters. Grbavica and Lukavica were under fierce Muslim heavy machine-gun fire, while Muslim snipers opened fire at the Serb communities of Rajlovac, Ilidza, Grbavica, the Ilidza-Vogosca and Pale-Sarajevo roads."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say about the Sarajevo battle-field being in jeopardy. Then in the second piece of news it says that the Muslim offensive had failed. And in the third report it is said that 3.000 Muslim fighters had been killed during the two-day offensive and that, on that day, another hundred of them were killed in Trnovo below Treskavica. Can you tell us this connecting point between the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Herzegovina Corps, where was it located geographically?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a small place called Trnovo and the defence positions were above it on the mountain. It was a very forbidding terrain, both in terms of launching attacks and defending it. In that particular area the Muslim forces attacked with the intention of breaking through the defence positions and caused the fall of one of most important municipalities which would probably create panic in the neighbouring municipality and facilitate the fall of the Serb civilians in the area. MUP forces, i.e., PJP companies, were often involved in the actions but they were subordinated to the VRS. But at all times there was insufficient forces to carry out that so we faced both successes and unsuccessful operation. We sometimes managed to close our ranks and invest superhuman efforts in order to prevent the fall that would be followed by an exodus and a massacre of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3756, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can't follow this on a day-by-day basis because I don't have time. Can we have 1D9122 now, dated the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yet again, General, the first news reported here concerns Sarajevo. I'll read this out in English. [In English] "Sarajevo - Muslim artillery attacked Serb positions in the north and north-west sections of the Sarajevo front - this being true especially for the areas of Vogosca and Srednje. The Muslims shelled residential buildings in Grbavica, though without causing casualties." [Interpretation] Is this consistent with your knowledge and recollection of these events?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. Since I was a member of the staff at Pale specifically charged with the Sarajevo battle-front, I was well informed and was eye-witness of artillery and infantry attacks day and night, of the assaults by the Muslim forces wishing to bring about the fall of the Serb positions. The SRNA agency reports on this again. This strategic axis from Central Bosnia in the direction of Sarajevo was another line of attack, Vogosca, et cetera, are also being mentioned. At one point in time the lines were broken through; however, as far as I can remember, it was precisely the special brigade forces that managed to counter these forces that had by this time entered deep into the territory. They managed to repel the attack and literally save the lives of tens of thousands of inhabitants of Ilijas, Vogosca, Srednje, and the entire area there. This report from the SRNA agency substantiates this, and of course my memory of this is very clear because I was engaged on this score. We were mustering the forces of the staff both in terms of the possible evacuation and combat to prevent any falling of the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is news concerning Srebrenica here as well, but you did say you weren't involved in this, although they are listing two or three pieces of news there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure of the purpose of that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was precisely trying to explain why I wasn't putting this question to the General here, because he was informed about the events in Sarajevo. It was for the benefit of the parties that I said that there is news here concerning Srebrenica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just don't think he needs to explain to the witness why he's not asking a question and build into his explanation the suggestion again that you weren't informed about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3757, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D9123. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, kindly look at the third paragraph that I'll read out in English. [In English] "Sarajevo - Muslim units continued opening artillery and sniper fire at residential areas of Srpsko Sarajevo, reported the general headquarters of VRS Information Service. In the RS Army Herzegovina Corps zone of responsibility, Muslim units used howitzer and 120-millimetre mortars against Serb lines of defence in Brdo and Hotovlje, in the Kalinovik war-zone. Muslim units opened machine-gun fire at Ravnice in the Mostarsko-Nevesinjski war-zone ..." and so on. And there are other reports from the -- another battle-field. There are a lot of reports and it seems that another battle-field was active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can see how to some extent this is justified by the cross about what he was focusing on at the time and whether he would have discussed Srebrenica, but it's a massively leading way - I haven't objected up until now - to just read out these documents and then ask him if that confirms with what he knew or if this is correct.
